performers: Carl Martin Öhmann, tenor; Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam; Carl Schuricht (live; Kerstin Thorborg sings the alto songs of the same concert)
intro: The wine is ready, but the singer insists on a song about death before anyone drinks. Carl Martin Öhmann and Carl Schuricht open Das Lied von der Erde in Amsterdam in 1939 with blaring horns and a refrain that climbs a semitone each time it returns.

sections.mNote: The tenor sings against horns and flutter-tongued flutes

sections.label: B · The gardens lie waste

sections.label: R · Dark is life, dark is death

sections.label: C · The host’s cellar and lute

sections.label: R′ · The refrain rises to A♭ minor

cues.title: Horns before the wine
cues.text: The horns throw out a three-note call. Flutes flutter-tongue, trumpets rattle behind their mutes, and Öhmann has to sing high against the orchestra. The heading is Allegro pesante: fast music with heavy feet.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Das Lied von der Erde, Universal Edition full score (1912), pp. 3–5: Allegro pesante, muted trumpets and the tenor’s entry. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/65/IMSLP20582-PMLP47886-Mahler_-_Das_Lied_von_der_Erde_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The garden laid waste
cues.text: “Wenn der Kummer naht” — when sorrow draws near. The boast falls quiet. A solo violin and the harps accompany a garden in which joy and song wither; Mahler marks the voice “düster, zart” — gloomy, tender.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition full score (1912), pp. 9–11, rehearsal figures 7–9. Hans Bethge’s text, adapted by Mahler; our translations.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The first dark refrain
cues.text: “Dunkel ist das Leben, ist der Tod” — dark is life, dark is death. The tenor’s refrain rests in G minor, with solo horn and harp arpeggios around it. Each later return lifts the same sentence one semitone higher.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 11–12. Christian Utz, Musicologica Austriaca (2018), section 3, identifies the three refrain keys: https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37. Bethge’s words; our translation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Back to the cellar
cues.text: The horns’ call and flutter-tongued flutes burst back at Tempo I subito. The next stanza addresses the host and his well-stocked cellar. The singer brings a lute; he considers a full cup worth more than all the kingdoms of the earth.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 13–21, orchestral return and Bethge’s second stanza as adapted by Mahler.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One semitone higher
cues.text: The second refrain climbs to A♭ minor. Öhmann has the same words, now a little higher in the throat. Schuricht lets these refrains move much more slowly than the drinking music around them.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 21–22. Utz, section 3 and Table 4, documents the refrain keys and Schuricht’s markedly slower refrain tempos: https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The orchestra takes the floor
cues.text: The tenor falls silent for a long interlude. An oboe comes forward, flutes flutter-tongue, and a muted trumpet picks out its notes above plucked strings. The music gathers into A♭ major before the voice returns.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 23–26, rehearsal figures 25–30; Utz, Table 2, bars 203–260. https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The sky stays blue
cues.text: “Das Firmament blaut ewig” — the heavens are blue for ever. Öhmann’s line places the earth’s returning spring beside the short human life. The strings have just sung out at full strength; the tenor answers quietly, marked passionate.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, p. 26, rehearsal figures 30–31: strings sempre ff and tenor p ma appassionato. Bethge’s words as set by Mahler; our translation. This is an existing cue for the passage.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Moonlight on the graves
cues.text: The opening fanfares return with glockenspiel, triangle and muted brass. The tenor points towards a shape crouching on the graves: an ape, howling into the sweet scent of life. The drinking song has become a nightmare.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 31–35, rehearsal figures 39–44. Utz, section 3, discusses the return of the opening music at bar 326: https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Schuricht empties the cup
cues.text: At last the singer permits the wine. The toast opens in A major before the final dark refrain. Schuricht stretches the emptying of the cup almost to a standstill: Öhmann takes his time over “zu Grund” — to the bottom.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 35–37. Utz, section 3 and video example 5, analyses this recording’s extreme ritardando at bar 381: https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37. Our translation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Death leaves a dissonance
cues.text: The final refrain reaches A minor. On the last “Tod” — death — Mahler leaves a diminished-seventh chord above the tonic bass. Then the horns and flutes reclaim the opening tempo, and the orchestra ends the song with a short, hard chord.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 37–38, rehearsal 48 onwards. Utz, section 3, discusses the diminished seventh at bar 393 and the short final chord: https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A solo violin after the boast
transitions.from: A · Horns and the golden cup
transitions.how: The sustained ending of the first boast softens into Sempre l’istesso tempo — still the same pace. Quiet strings and harps surround “Wenn der Kummer naht”; the solo violin soon adds a coaxing phrase. Mahler marks the tenor düster, zart.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition full score (1912), pp. 8–10, rehearsal figures 6–8.

transitions.title: The harp slows into G minor
transitions.to: R · Dark is life, dark is death
transitions.how: Zurückhaltend. Ruhig. holds back the end of the garden stanza. Harp arpeggios replace the repeated chords, and a solo horn accompanies the refrain in G minor. The tenor’s line is marked sehr getragen — very sustained.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 11–12, rehearsal figures 10–11; refrain key in Utz, section 3. https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37

transitions.title: The horns break into the refrain
transitions.from: R · Dark is life, dark is death
transitions.to: C · The host’s cellar and lute
transitions.how: The held “Tod” meets a diminished-seventh chord over G. Tempo I subito then restores the horn call, flutter-tongued flutes and glockenspiel. Open trumpets join the renewed fanfare as the strings break into repeated notes.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 12–13, rehearsal 12. Utz identifies the chord over the tonic bass at bar 90: https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37

transitions.title: The same words rise a semitone
transitions.from: C · The host’s cellar and lute
transitions.to: R′ · The refrain rises to A♭ minor
transitions.how: The wine stanza ends on “Reiche dieser Erde”. A ritardando leads into a tempo, sehr ruhig, with harp arpeggios and plucked bass. The second refrain moves the first refrain’s G minor up to A♭ minor; the strings remain muted through its approach.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 21–22, rehearsal 23; refrain keys in Utz, section 3. https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37

transitions.title: A muted trumpet takes over
transitions.from: R′ · The refrain rises to A♭ minor
transitions.to: Dev · The orchestra beneath an endless sky
transitions.how: The refrain’s held notes run into an orchestral interlude in the A♭ region. An oboe projects above the fading winds. At a tempo, plucked strings and harp chords begin again, followed by a muted trumpet and flutter-tongued flutes.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition score, p. 23, rehearsal 25; Utz, Table 2, orchestral interlude. https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37

transitions.title: The opening returns on the graves
transitions.from: Dev · The orchestra beneath an endless sky
transitions.to: A′ · The ape on the graves
transitions.how: The tenor finishes the line about earth’s rotten trinkets. A rising woodwind rush brings back the opening fanfare, with glockenspiel, triangle and muted trumpets. The low strings strike plucked notes as the tenor turns towards the graves.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 31–32, rehearsal figures 39–40. Utz discusses the opening’s return at bar 326: https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37

transitions.title: A-major wine after the howl
transitions.from: A′ · The ape on the graves
transitions.to: R″ · The cups are finally emptied
transitions.how: Brass raise their bells for the ape’s howl, with cymbal and bass drum beneath. The following ritardando brings the toast into A major. Winds and horns sustain as the tenor finally tells the company to drink; harp figures accompany the slowing phrase.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 35–37, rehearsal figures 44–47; Utz, section 3, expanded final refrain. https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37

transitions.title: A diminished chord, then the horns
transitions.from: R″ · The cups are finally emptied
transitions.how: The last refrain settles into A minor, but its final “Tod” lands on a diminished-seventh chord over A. Tempo I releases the horns’ opening call and the high woodwinds. The orchestra carries the dissonance straight into its short final outburst.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 37–38, rehearsal 48; diminished seventh at bar 393 in Utz, section 3. https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37

source.title: Mahler, Das Lied von der Erde, I. Das Trinklied vom Jammer der Erde, full score (Universal Edition, 1912, plate U.E. 3637)
source.locator: Printed pp. 3–38: opening fanfares, three refrains, the ape scene and orchestral postlude.

timeline.note: The horns’ three-note call meets flutter-tongued flutes and rapidly tongued muted trumpets.
The tenor enters mit voller Kraft against the full orchestra.
Wenn der Kummer naht: a hushed stanza with harps and a solo violin.
The first refrain: sehr ruhig, a solo horn, harp arpeggios and held strings.
The opening tempo returns with flutter-tongued flutes, open trumpets and repeated string notes.
The tenor addresses the host above trombones and glockenspiel.
Harp patterns suggest the lute; woodwinds and trombones sustain beneath.
Two solo violins and a solo cello accompany the wine toast, with muted trumpets.
The second refrain, sehr ruhig, a semitone higher; mutes come off the strings.
The orchestra alone: flutter-tongued flutes, a prominent oboe and marcato trumpet figures.
Violins and violas play sempre ff, using the G string, before the voice returns.
The tenor sings Das Firmament blaut ewig over soft winds and strings.
The tenor rests while winds and strings carry the melody through F minor.
Harps and trilling woodwinds surround the tenor’s passionate question, “Du aber, Mensch”.
Seht dort hinab: trills, brass and snapped strings surround the tenor’s cry.
Muted trumpets, glockenspiel and triangle sound the howl.
The climax: brass with bells up, cymbal and bass drum.
Jetzt nehmt den Wein: a quieter A-major toast with harps and horns.
Schuricht slows the emptying of the cup; the harps accompany the final refrain.
A fortissimo Tempo I postlude for the orchestra alone ends the song.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Carl Martin Öhmann (tenor), Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam (orchestra), Carl Schuricht (conductor)
fields.note: The item credits Kerstin Thorborg (alto), Carl Martin Öhmann (tenor) and Carl Schuricht (conductor) for the whole concert, and names the singer on each track; Kerstin Thorborg does not sing in this song. The Mahler Foundation’s discography lists the same three with the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam. The orchestra was not yet styled “Royal” in 1939.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The item does not say which score edition the orchestra used or whether any passage was cut. The first edition (Universal Edition, 1912) is the score read for the notes on this page; the 1939 performing materials may differ.

fields.label: Recorded

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Music by Gustav Mahler (died 1911); words adapted by Mahler from Hans Bethge’s Die chinesische Flöte (Bethge died 1946), itself a paraphrase of Tang-dynasty poems by way of French and German translations. The 1912 first edition is hosted on IMSLP as public domain.
fields.note: A term calculation (life plus 70 years; Bethge’s text has been free in life-plus-70 jurisdictions since 2017), not a clearance of every edition or translation.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Treated as public domain in the European Union (territorial): a live broadcast of 5 October 1939 whose related rights, on the sources consulted, had expired before the extended terms applied on 1 November 2013. United States status is not established.
fields.note: Before the 2011 extension, Directive 2006/116/EC gave performers and phonogram producers 50-year terms. For a performance of 1939 the performer’s term ran 50 years from the performance, to 1989, unless a fixation of it in a phonogram was lawfully published or lawfully communicated to the public within that period, which would have started a longer term from that event. The live radio broadcast was a communication of the performance, not of a phonogram fixation, and the sources consulted document no earlier publication of the acetate fixation; the date of its first issue on disc is not given in them, so this is an inference, not a clearance. Directive 2011/77/EU lengthened terms to 70 years only for rights still protected on 1 November 2013 (Article 10(5)), so rights that had already expired were not revived. The item carries a Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s statement and not the basis used here.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
